about: Five short lessons for tauhud.com/learn. The page loads them; `up tau` on the server asks the engine every try and every solution and prints ok or FAIL, so the expected answers here are checked against the real engine. A task's `fill` is the fill-in shown to people who picked 'never written a formula': the pattern with ▢ and the choices for it. `guide` is the step-by-step tour shown to people who picked 'never written a formula': one idea per card, every question is a try or solution of the lessons above, so the self-test already checks it; for a guess, the engine's answer decides which choice was right. A lesson with "level": "pro" is shown only to people who picked 'I know logic or Tau'. `asked` holds questions from the community in IDNI's monthly Q&A videos, answered in our own words; a `try` is always a lesson try, so the self-test covers it. `brief` feeds tauhud.com/learn/brief/: a short software brief, each requirement in plain English with the Tau line written for it by hand; `checks` lists which requirements are switched on and the verdict the engine must give, and the self-test asks each of them.

lessons.title: Yes or no
lessons.text: Tau answers questions about formulas. sat asks: can this be true? A letter such as x is a variable, and the formula counts as true when some value of x makes it true.

tries.label: Can x be 0?
tries.says: T: yes, x = 0 can be true.

tries.label: Can x be 0 and 1?
tries.says: F: no value of x is 0 and 1 at once.

tries.label: Why not?
tries.says: Tau names the smallest set of parts that already contradict each other.

task.text: Change x = 0 && x = 1 so that Tau answers T again. Hint: && means and, || means or.

lessons.title: True in every case
lessons.text: valid asks the harder question: is this true whatever the values are? sat is happy with one way to make it true, valid needs all of them.

tries.label: Is x = 0 always true?
tries.says: F: x could be something else.

tries.label: Is x 0 or not 0?
tries.says: T: whatever x is, it is 0 or it is not.

task.text: Write a formula with && in it that is still valid.

lessons.title: Inputs in, outputs out
lessons.text: A testnet rule reads inputs and writes outputs, one step at a time. i1[t] is input 1 at step t, o1[t] is output 1. :bv[8] makes them 8-bit numbers, 0 to 255, and { 1 } is the number 1. run feeds the inputs in and shows what Tau writes.

tries.label: Add one
tries.says: At every step Tau writes the input plus one.

tries.label: Past 255
tries.says: 8-bit numbers wrap around: 255 + 1 is 0. A rule that must not wrap has to say so itself.

task.text: Make o1 twice the input. Run it with the inputs 1, 2, 3.

lessons.title: Promises over time
lessons.text: A spec is a promise for every step. always must hold at each step, sometimes at one step at least. Tau checks the promise against every input anyone could send, and [t-1] reads the step before.

tries.label: Will the input ever be 1?
tries.says: F: the input may stay 0 forever, and the spec cannot force it.

tries.label: Will the output ever copy it?
tries.says: T: the output can copy the input at the step it reads it.

tries.label: Grow forever?
tries.says: F: an output that must grow at every step runs out of 2-bit numbers (0 to 3).

task.text: Change the last one so it can hold forever: the output only has to differ from the step before.

lessons.title: A real testnet rule
lessons.text: Every rule on the testnet is a spec like this one. For each transfer the node feeds the amount in on i1, and the rule answers on o5: 1 lets the transfer through, 0 stops it. This rule stops anything over 1,000.

tries.label: 500, then 5,000
tries.says: 500 goes through (1), 5,000 is stopped (0).

task.text: Lower the limit to 100 and run 500 again: now it should be stopped.

lessons.title: Terms and formulas
lessons.text: Tau has two layers. Terms are Boolean functions built with & (and), | (or), ' (complement) and ^ (xor); x y is x & y, and 0 and 1 are bottom and top of the algebra. Formulas relate terms with = != <= and join them with && || ! -> <->. Untyped variables live in the default type tau.

tries.label: x ≤ y means x y' = 0
tries.says: T: in any Boolean algebra, x is below y exactly when x meets the complement of y in 0.

tries.label: Two tops that meet in 0?
tries.says: F: 1 & 1 is 1, never 0.

tries.label: Which parts clash?
tries.says: The core names the parts that already contradict each other.

task.text: Write a valid formula that uses the complement '.

lessons.title: all and ex
lessons.text: all x and ex x quantify a variable over the algebra. A free variable is read existentially by sat, so sat x = 0 already means ex x x = 0. The default algebra tau is atomless, so it has many more elements than 0 and 1.

tries.label: Is every x zero?
tries.says: F: the algebra has elements other than 0.

tries.label: Every x has a complement
tries.spec: all x ex y x & y = 0 && x | y = 1
tries.says: T: y = x' meets x in 0 and joins it to 1.

task.text: Change all x x = 0 so that it holds, with one word.

lessons.title: For all inputs, some output
lessons.text: sat on a spec with streams is not plain satisfiability: every input is quantified for all, every output exists, in time order, and outputs may depend on inputs of the same step. So a spec cannot constrain its inputs, and it must answer whatever comes in. realizable asks the same question for full LTL.

tries.label: Demand the input
tries.says: F: the input is chosen by the environment and may be anything else.

tries.label: Answer with the complement
tries.says: T: whatever comes in, the output can be its complement.

tries.label: Copy it and be 0
tries.says: F: once the input is not 0, no output does both.

tries.label: Copy, as realizable
tries.says: T: a strategy exists that answers every input.

task.text: Change one connective in o1[t] = i1[t] && o1[t] = 0 so that sat answers T.

guide.title: A formula is a statement
guide.text: A formula is a short statement that is either true or false, like “the light is on”. Tau writes it with letters and signs. The letter x is a box that can hold a value.
guide.ask: Can the box hold 0? Ask the real Tau engine.
guide.says: Tau answers T for yes and F for no. Here: yes, x can be 0.

guide.title: Two statements joined by and
guide.text: You can join two statements into one with && (read it: and). The joined statement is only true when both halves are true, like “it is raining and the sun is shining”. Here both halves talk about the same box x.
guide.ask: Your guess: can x be 0 and 1 at the same time?
guide.says: x cannot be 0 and 1 at once: a box holds one value at a time, so the two halves are never true together.

guide.title: Joined by or instead
guide.text: Now join the same two halves with || (read it: or). Then one true half is enough, like “I take the bus or I walk”. Pick the sign that makes Tau say yes.
guide.says: With or, x = 0 is enough. You just wrote your first Tau formula.

guide.title: True for every value
guide.text: Until now Tau looked for one value of x that works. A stronger question is: is it true whatever x is? Tau calls that valid. The sign != means “is not”.
guide.ask: Your guess: is this true whatever x is?
guide.says: Any x is either 0 or not 0, so this holds every time.

guide.title: A rule is a little machine
guide.text: On the testnet a rule reads a number that comes in and writes a number that goes out, one step at a time. i1 is the number in, o1 the number out. This machine adds one.
guide.ask: Run it with the numbers 1, 2 and 3.
guide.says: Every number that goes in comes out one bigger.

guide.title: Numbers have a size
guide.text: These numbers have 8 bits, so they go from 0 to 255 and no further.
guide.ask: Your guess: what comes out when 255 goes in?
guide.says: Like a trip counter, it rolls over to 0 after 255. A rule that must not roll over has to say so itself.

guide.title: A real testnet rule
guide.text: Every transfer on the testnet passes a rule like this one. The amount comes in, and the rule answers 1 to let it through or 0 to stop it. This one stops anything over 1,000.
guide.ask: Your guess: what happens to a transfer of 5,000?
guide.says: 500 goes through, 5,000 is stopped. You just read a real testnet rule.

asked.q: Do I have to learn Boolean algebra to use Tau?
asked.a: No. The guide on this page uses none: you compare things with = and join them with and (&&) and or (||). Boolean algebra is what Tau does underneath; it helps later, when you want to know why an answer is what it is.

asked.q: How does Tau tell an input from an output?
asked.a: By the name: a stream whose name starts with i is an input, one that starts with o is an output, unless the spec declares it otherwise. Inputs come from outside, so a spec cannot demand them; outputs are what the spec decides.
asked.says: F: the spec cannot decide what comes in.

asked.q: What goes inside the curly brackets?
asked.a: A constant of a given type: { 1 }:bv[8] is the number 1 as an 8-bit value. Without braces, 1 means all bits on, so 1:bv[8] is 255.
asked.says: Every number that goes in comes out one bigger.

asked.q: Does always mean the rule has to hold forever?
asked.a: Yes: at every step, on a timeline without an end. A spec without always or sometimes is read as always. That is why a promise that cannot last forever gets an F.
asked.says: F: an output that must grow at every step runs out of 2-bit numbers (0 to 3).

asked.q: How do I switch from step-by-step code to Tau?
asked.a: Stop writing steps and write what must be true. o1[t] = i1[t] + 1 is not an order to add; it is a promise about every step, and Tau finds the outputs that keep it.
asked.says: Every number that goes in comes out one bigger.

asked.a: True in every case, whatever the values are. sat is happy with one way to make it true.
asked.says: F: x could be something else.

asked.a: It rewrites a formula into a simplest equivalent form that Tau can work with. In the tau REPL on your computer, normalize shows that form; this page answers sat, valid, why and run.

asked.q: When can I try Tau in a web browser?
asked.a: IDNI answers this in the video. Until then, this page sends your formula to a real Tau engine on tauhud's server, so you can try it here.

asked.q: How do I get better at writing Tau rules?
asked.a: Practice on small rules. Lesson 5 changes a real testnet limit, and the Rule Playground runs a rule against the testnet's own checks.
